messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 37-year-old database administrator, had always prided himself on his physical health. That changed abruptly two years ago when a sudden, severe respiratory infection landed him in the intensive care unit for ten days. He remembered the suffocating sensation of the ventilator, the beeping monitors that never stopped, and the cold panic of a doctor’s face as they inserted a chest tube. What stayed with him most, though, was the moment he couldn’t catch his breath—a feeling of being trapped in his own body, certain he was dying. The medical team saved his life, but the experience left an invisible scar.

In the months that followed, David’s world began to shrink. He noticed his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, as if a switch had been left on. When he felt strong negative emotions—fear, anger, or shame—his chest would tighten, and he’d become hyperaware of his breathing. This physical reactivity made him feel that his body was betraying him, and he came to believe that any loss of control over his internal state could lead to disaster. To manage this, he began to adopt strict strategies. He stopped exercising entirely, because even a slight increase in his heart rate triggered the same suffocating panic he’d felt in the hospital. He also restricted his eating, controlling every calorie and meal time with meticulous precision, believing that if he could master his body’s inputs, he could prevent another collapse. He avoided any medical cues—hospitals, ambulances, even the sight of a stethoscope on a TV show—because they brought back the raw terror of those days.

These strategies, however, backfired. By avoiding exercise and eating so rigidly, David’s overall fitness declined. He became more sedentary, and his weight fluctuated. One afternoon at work, while sitting at his desk in the data center, he felt a sudden, inexplicable shortness of breath—a somatic trigger that sent him spiraling. He had to excuse himself to the bathroom, gripping the sink, convinced he was reliving the infection. He realized, with a sinking feeling, that his own efforts to stay safe were making him more vulnerable to these triggers. The more he avoided medical procedures or physical exertion, the more his body became a source of unpredictable alarms.

The cycle tightened. Each time a trigger—like the sight of a needle during a routine blood donation drive at his office—provoked a strong physical reaction, he felt his body on alert all over again. The threat felt immediate and real. In response, he doubled down on his maladaptive strategies: he stopped driving past the hospital on his commute, he skipped his annual physical, and he refused to go to the grocery store if he saw an ambulance parked outside. His wife, frustrated by his constant vigilance and refusal to seek medical care for a minor infection, eventually left him. David was now alone, his life organized around avoiding any reminder of that hospital room.

What finally brought him to therapy was a panic attack at his desk last week. He had been reviewing a routine system log, and the quiet hum of the computer fans reminded him of the ventilator. He couldn’t breathe. His supervisor found him hyperventilating. David was terrified that his mind was breaking, and he hoped, more than anything, that someone could teach him how to feel safe in his own skin again.
